verses.text: Elisha said, “Listen to the LORD's word. This is what the LORD says: ‘About this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel and two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel.’”

The officer the king was leaning on said to the man of God, “Even if the LORD opened windows in heaven, could that happen?” Elisha answered, “You'll see it with your own eyes, but you won't eat any of it.”
Four men with leprosy were at the entrance to the city gate. They asked each other, “Why sit here until we die?
If we go into the city, we'll die there in the famine. If we stay here, we'll die anyway. Let's go surrender to the Syrian army. If they spare us, we'll live. If they kill us, we'll die either way.”
They got up at dusk and headed for the Syrian camp. When they reached the edge of the camp, nobody was there.

The Lord had made the Syrian army hear the sound of chariots and horses, like the approach of a huge army. They said to each other, “The king of Israel must have hired the Hittite and Egyptian kings to attack us!”
So at dusk they ran for their lives, abandoning their tents, horses, and donkeys and leaving the camp just as it was.

When the four men reached the edge of the camp, they went into a tent and ate and drank. Then they carried away silver, gold, and clothes and hid them. They came back, went into another tent, and took things from there and hid those too.
Then they said to each other, “This isn't right. Today we have good news, and we're keeping it to ourselves. If we wait until morning, we'll be punished. Let's go tell the king's household now.”

They went and called to the city gatekeepers, “We went to the Syrian camp. There was nobody there, not even a voice. The horses and donkeys were still tied up, and the tents were just as they'd left them.”
The gatekeepers called out the news, and it was reported inside the palace.

The king got up in the night and told his servants, “I know what the Syrians are doing. They know we're starving. They've left the camp to hide in the fields. They're thinking, ‘When the people come out of the city, we'll capture them alive and get inside.’”

One of his servants said, “Let some men take five of the horses left in the city. They're as likely to die as the rest of Israel still here, just like all those who have already died. Let's send them to find out.”
They got two chariots with horses, and the king sent them after the Syrian army. “Go and see,” he said.
They followed the trail as far as the Jordan. The whole road was littered with clothes and equipment the Syrians had thrown away in their hurry. The messengers went back and told the king.
Then the people went out and plundered the Syrian camp. A seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, just as the LORD had said.
The king had put the officer he leaned on in charge of the gate. The crowd trampled him there, and he died, just as the man of God had said when the king came down to see him.
It happened just as the man of God had told the king: “About this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria, two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel and a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel.”
That officer had answered the man of God, “Even if the LORD opened windows in heaven, could it happen?” Elisha had said, “You'll see it with your own eyes, but you won't eat any of it.”
That's exactly what happened to him. The people trampled him at the gate, and he died.
